claims.text: FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles have been synthesized with a distribution of particle sizes.
A newly developed, composition-specific atomistic interatomic potential will enable molecular dynamics simulations of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
The new potential can be calibrated to accurately represent the energy landscape and atomic interactions of the multielement FeCuCrCoNi system.
Smaller nanoparticles have a higher surface-to-volume ratio.
The higher surface-to-volume ratio of smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles reduces their cohesive energy.
Reduced cohesive energy lowers the structural and thermal stability of smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
The tailored potential enables precise simulation of size-dependent surface effects in FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
The melting or major structural-transition temperature of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles decreases as particle size decreases.
Larger FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles or bulk material may exhibit a higher transition temperature than smaller nanoparticles.
The predicted size relationship is expected to apply only within the size range represented by the potential-calibration data.
Extremely small nanoparticles outside the calibration range may not follow the predicted trend.
Strong environmental interactions may alter the predicted size dependence of thermal stability.
The magnitude of the predicted transition-temperature decrease is uncertain because of simulation limitations, thermal fluctuations, and complex multielement interactions.
Molecular dynamics simulations can compare the thermal response of 3 nm, 5 nm, and 10 nm FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Differential scanning calorimetry or in situ TEM heating can provide complementary measurements of nanoparticle transition or melting temperatures.
A non-significant, non-monotonic, or opposite relationship between transition temperature and particle size would falsify the stated size-dependent hypothesis.
